o: We must implement a skiplist supporting `search`, `add`, and `erase` with expected $O(\log n)$ time per operation, handling duplicates. A skiplist is a hierarchy of sorted linked lists: the bottom layer contains all elements, and each higher layer is a sparser 'express lane' built by promoting nodes probabilistically. To search for a value we start at the top-left head node and move right while the next value is smaller than (or equal to) the target, otherwise drop down a level; this visits only $O(\log n)$ nodes in expectation. For `add` we record the path of predecessors at each level, insert the new node at level 0, then randomly promote it upward, linking it into each recorded predecessor's next pointer. For `erase` we find all levels where the value appears and unlink it; if it never existed we return false. Constraints are small (values up to 2·10⁴, 5·10⁴ calls), so even simpler structures would pass, but the skiplist is what the problem asks us to build.
k: A skiplist is layered sorted linked lists; searching walks right while smaller, then drops down, giving expected O(log n).
During search/add/erase, remember the predecessor ('update') node at every level so insertion/removal only rewires next pointers.
Node height is chosen by repeated coin flips (e.g., while rand() < 0.5), so no rebalancing logic is ever needed.
Duplicates are handled naturally: erase removes one matching node per level where it exists.

a.i: Each node stores its value and an array of `next` pointers whose length equals its random height. A sentinel head of fixed MAX_LEVEL height anchors every layer. All three operations first perform the classic descent from the top level, recording the last node visited at each level (`update`). Insertion links the new node after those predecessors and promotes it with probability 1/2 per level; erasure unlinks the node wherever found. Because each level halves the expected number of nodes, the expected work per operation is $O(\log n)$.
s: Define Node(value, level) holding val and next array; create head with MAX_LEVEL null pointers.
search: from top level, move right while cur.next[i] exists and cur.next[i].val < target (or <= for finding exact node); drop down; return whether bottom-layer successor equals target.
add: run the descent recording update[i]; create node with height h = 1 + coin flips; link it into levels 0..h-1 after update[i].
erase: descend with condition < num to find predecessors; let node = update[0].next[0]; if missing or val != num return false; else unlink node at every level where update[i].next[i] == node.
a.t: Expected O(log n) per operation — each level halves the number of candidate nodes, so the descent touches O(log n) nodes on average.
a.sp: O(n) expected total space — each element occupies ~2 pointers on average due to geometric height distribution.

a.n: Approach 2: Fixed-Height / Deterministic-Layer Skiplist (bucketed by value range)
a.i: Since values are bounded by 2·10⁴, we can use a simplified deterministic variant: keep a single sorted linked list plus a coarse index array that stores a pointer to every k-th node (e.g., every 64 nodes). Search jumps through the index first, then scans at most k nodes. This keeps code short and gives worst-case O(n/k + k) ≈ O(√n)-ish behavior, which easily fits constraints, though it degrades under many inserts unless the index is rebuilt periodically.
s: Maintain a sorted singly linked list with dummy head, plus an index array rebuilt lazily when size doubles.
search/add/erase: walk the index to jump close to the target, then scan the base list linearly within the block.
add inserts in sorted position; erase unlinks if found; rebuild index when size crosses a power-of-two threshold.
a.t: O(size/step + step) worst case per operation (~O(√n) with step≈√n); amortized rebuild cost is O(size) every doubling of size.
a.sp: O(n) for the list plus O(size/step) for the index array.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 — it is the canonical answer and directly demonstrates understanding of probabilistic data structures; Approach 2 is a pragmatic fallback worth mentioning if you struggle with multi-level wiring. Common pitfalls: (1) using `<` vs `<=` inconsistently between search and erase — use strict `<` during descent and check equality on the bottom-level successor; (2) forgetting to unlink the erased node at *every* level it appears; (3) off-by-one errors in the update-array indexing; (4) infinite loops when the promotion loop lacks a MAX_LEVEL cap. Edge cases: duplicates (erase removes exactly one occurrence), erasing/searching values absent from the structure, and operations on an empty skiplist. Likely follow-ups: how to make it concurrent-safe (lock-free skiplists via CAS), how to support range queries or `count(num)` (store counts per node), and why expected O(log n) holds (geometric height distribution with parameter p=1/2).
